910.name: Ancient Baltic Peoples of Latvia
910.description: The territory of modern Latvia was settled after the last Ice Age by Baltic and Finno-Ugric peoples. The Latgalians, Selonians, Semigallians, and Curonians developed distinct tribal cultures, while the Finno-Ugric Livonians gave their name to the broader region of Livonia.

sub_clusters.name: Mesolithic & Neolithic Latvia
sub_clusters.description: Post-glacial settlement of the Latvian coast and river valleys. The Kunda culture, the transition to agriculture, and the emergence of distinct Baltic and Finno-Ugric linguistic groups along the Daugava, Gauja, and Venta rivers.

sub_clusters.name: Bronze & Iron Age Baltic Tribes
sub_clusters.description: The differentiation of the Latgalian, Selonian, Semigallian, and Curonian tribes. Hillforts, amber trade, and contacts with the Roman world along the 'Amber Road'. The distinctive Baltic tribal cultures and their relationship with neighbouring Slavic, Finnic, and Scandinavian peoples.

sub_clusters.name: Viking Age & the Livonians
sub_clusters.description: Curonian pirates and Viking-age trade along the Daugava. The Finno-Ugric Livonians at the mouth of the Daugava, early contacts with Scandinavian and Rus' merchants, and the first German missionary attempts by Meinhard of Segeberg (c. 1184).

920.name: The Livonian Crusade & the Founding of Riga
920.description: Bishop Albert founded Riga (1201) and launched the Livonian Crusade. The Sword Brothers and later the Livonian Order conquered the Baltic tribes. The Battle of Saule (1236) against the Samogitians was a turning point. German rule and Christianisation transformed Latvian society.

sub_clusters.name: The Founding of Riga & the Crusade
sub_clusters.description: Bishop Albert of Buxtehude founded Riga (1201) as the base for the Northern Crusade. The Livonian Brothers of the Sword systematically conquered the Livonians, Latgalians, and Selonians. Indigenous resistance and forced baptism.
key_events: Founding of Riga by Bishop Albert (1201)

sub_clusters.name: Battle of Saule & Conquest of the Curonians
sub_clusters.description: The decisive Battle of Saule (1236) — the Samogitians and Semigallians destroyed the Livonian Brothers of the Sword. The order merged with the Teutonic Knights. The prolonged conquest of the Semigallians (completed 1290) and Curonians. The emergence of the Livonian Confederation.
key_events: Battle of Saule — defeat of the Livonian Sword Brothers (1236)

920.name: The Livonian Confederation & Hanseatic Riga
920.description: Latvia formed the core of the Livonian Confederation under the Livonian Order, the Archbishop of Riga, and other ecclesiastical lords. Riga flourished as a major Hanseatic trading city, while Latvian peasants were progressively enserfed under the Baltic German landowning class.

sub_clusters.name: Livonian Order & German Baltic Nobility
sub_clusters.description: The Livonian Order governed much of Latvia. Baltic German nobles controlled estates and politics. Latvian peasants faced deepening serfdom. The construction of great castles at Cēsis, Bauska, and Turaida. Conflicts between the Order and the Archbishop of Riga.

sub_clusters.name: Hanseatic Riga & Medieval Commerce
sub_clusters.description: Riga as one of the foremost Hanseatic cities, controlling trade between Russia and Western Europe along the Daugava. The House of the Blackheads, St Peter's Church, and the prosperous German merchant community. The Reformation's arrival in the 1520s.

930.name: Polish-Lithuanian & Swedish Rule
930.description: After the Livonian War dissolved the Confederation, Latvia was partitioned: Courland became a Polish-Lithuanian vassal duchy, while Riga and Vidzeme (Livland) passed to Sweden. The Duchy of Courland under the Kettler dynasty briefly became a colonial power.

sub_clusters.name: The Livonian War & Partition of Latvia
sub_clusters.description: Ivan the Terrible's invasion of Livonia, the dissolution of the Livonian Confederation, and the partition of Latvian territory. Courland became a duchy under Polish-Lithuanian suzerainty under the last Master, Gotthard Kettler.

sub_clusters.name: The Duchy of Courland & Colonial Ventures
sub_clusters.description: The remarkable Duchy of Courland under Duke Jacob Kettler (r. 1642–82): shipbuilding, iron works, and colonial possessions in Tobago and Gambia. The duchy's golden age as a small but prosperous Baltic state.
key_events: Courland establishes colonies in Tobago and Gambia (1651–54)

sub_clusters.name: Swedish Vidzeme & the Counter-Reformation
sub_clusters.description: Swedish conquest of Riga and Vidzeme (1629). The Swedish period brought some peasant protections and educational initiatives, though the Jesuit Counter-Reformation had previously strengthened Catholicism in Latgale under Polish rule.

930.name: Russian Imperial Era in Latvia
930.description: Peter the Great conquered Riga and Vidzeme in the Great Northern War. Courland was absorbed by Russia in 1795. The Baltic German Ritterschaft governed local affairs while Latvian peasants endured serfdom until emancipation (1817–61).

sub_clusters.name: Russian Conquest & the Great Plague
sub_clusters.description: The devastating Great Northern War, the siege and capture of Riga (1710), the plague that killed over half the population of Vidzeme, and the Treaty of Nystad (1721) incorporating Latvian territories into the Russian Empire.

sub_clusters.name: Serfdom, Herrnhuters & Emancipation
sub_clusters.description: The Gutswirtschaft system of Baltic German serfdom, the Moravian Brethren (Herrnhuter) movement bringing literacy and religious awakening to Latvian peasants, the emancipation laws of 1817 (Courland) and 1819 (Vidzeme) freeing peasants without land, and gradual land reform.

940.name: The Latvian National Awakening
940.description: The Latvian national awakening (Atmoda) forged modern national identity through language, literature, song festivals, and journalism. The 'Young Latvians' (Jaunlatvieši) challenged Baltic German cultural hegemony and built the foundations of national consciousness.

sub_clusters.name: The Young Latvians & Cultural Awakening
sub_clusters.description: Krišjānis Valdemārs, Krišjānis Barons, and the Jaunlatvieši movement. The first Latvian Song Festival (Dziesmu svētki) in Riga (1873), the collection of dainas (folk songs), the founding of Latvian-language newspapers, and the creation of a national literary tradition.

sub_clusters.name: The New Current & Russification
sub_clusters.description: The Jaunā strāva (New Current) movement introducing socialist ideas, the poetry of Rainis and Aspazija, Alexander III's Russification policies suppressing both German and Latvian culture, and the growing tensions between the Baltic German elite, Russian administrators, and Latvian nationalists.

940.name: Revolution & the Road to Independence
940.description: The 1905 Revolution erupted violently in Latvia — the most radical in the Russian Empire. World War I devastated the country, with the Latvian Riflemen fighting heroically. The collapse of Russia and Germany created the opportunity for Latvian independence (18 November 1918).

sub_clusters.name: The 1905 Revolution in Latvia
sub_clusters.description: Latvia experienced the most intense revolutionary violence in the entire Russian Empire. Worker strikes in Riga, the burning of over 300 Baltic German manor houses, punitive expeditions, and mass emigration of revolutionaries. The forging of Latvian political consciousness.

sub_clusters.name: World War I & the Latvian Riflemen
sub_clusters.description: Latvia as a major Eastern Front battlefield, the formation of the Latvian Rifle battalions (strēlnieki) fighting for Russia, the German occupation of Courland (1915) and then all of Latvia (1918), and the People's Council's declaration of independence (18 November 1918).

950.name: Latvian Independence & the Interwar Republic
950.description: The Latvian War of Independence (1918–20) secured statehood against Bolsheviks, German Freikorps, and White Russians. The interwar Republic achieved radical land reform, democratic governance, and cultural flourishing before Ulmanis's authoritarian coup (1934).

sub_clusters.name: Latvian War of Independence
sub_clusters.description: Fighting on multiple fronts: the Bolshevik advance and the Latvian Socialist Soviet Republic, the German Freikorps and Andrievs Niedra's puppet government, the decisive Battle of Cēsis (June 1919) with Estonian support, and the Latgale campaign. The Latvian-Soviet peace treaty of 1920.

sub_clusters.name: Interwar Democracy & Land Reform
sub_clusters.description: The radical 1920 land reform dismantling Baltic German estates, the democratic Saeima, cultural autonomy for minorities, the founding of the University of Latvia, and the vibrant cultural and intellectual life of interwar Riga.

sub_clusters.name: The Ulmanis Authoritarian Era
sub_clusters.description: Kārlis Ulmanis's bloodless coup (15 May 1934), the suppression of parties and parliament, nationalist economic policies ('Latvia for Latvians'), and the growing geopolitical threat. The Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact sealed Latvia's fate.

950.name: Soviet & Nazi Occupation
950.description: Latvia endured Soviet occupation (1940–41), Nazi occupation (1941–45) with the devastation of the Holocaust, and renewed Soviet occupation (1945–91). Mass deportations, the Forest Brothers resistance, collectivisation, and heavy Russian immigration transformed Latvian demographics.

sub_clusters.name: First Soviet Occupation & the Year of Terror
sub_clusters.description: Soviet occupation (June 1940), the staged elections and annexation, the 'Year of Terror' — nationalisation, NKVD arrests, and the devastating deportation of 14 June 1941 sending over 15,000 Latvians to Siberia, including the Ulmanis government.

sub_clusters.name: Nazi Occupation & the Holocaust
sub_clusters.description: German invasion (July 1941), the Reichskommissariat Ostland. The Holocaust in Latvia: the Rumbula massacre (November–December 1941) killing over 25,000 Jews, the Riga Ghetto, the Latvian SS Legion, and the massive civilian losses.

sub_clusters.name: Stalinist Era & the Forest Brothers
sub_clusters.description: The second Soviet occupation, the massive March 1949 deportation of over 42,000 Latvians, forced collectivisation, and the Forest Brothers (meža brāļi) partisan resistance. The destruction of Latvian cultural and economic independence.

sub_clusters.name: Soviet Latvia & Russification
sub_clusters.description: Post-Stalin thaw, massive industrial immigration of Russian-speakers (Latvians becoming a near-minority in their own country), environmental activism (against the Daugavpils hydroelectric dam), and the underground preservation of national culture.

960.name: The Baltic Way & Modern Latvia
960.description: The Latvian Popular Front, the Baltic Way (1989), and the restoration of independence (1991). Latvia navigated the transition to democracy and market economy, joined NATO and the EU (2004), and addressed its complex demographic legacy while building a modern European state.

sub_clusters.name: The Latvian Independence Movement
sub_clusters.description: Environmental protests, the Latvian Popular Front (Tautas Fronte), the Baltic Way human chain (23 August 1989), the barricade days of January 1991 defending key buildings against Soviet OMON forces, and the restoration of independence (21 August 1991).
key_events: Baltic Way — 2 million people form a human chain across the Baltic states (23 August 1989)

sub_clusters.name: Transition & EU Integration
sub_clusters.description: Economic transition and privatisation, the citizenship and language laws addressing the large Russian-speaking minority, the restoration of the Saeima, NATO and EU accession negotiations, and the painful process of lustration and historical reckoning.

sub_clusters.name: Contemporary Latvia
sub_clusters.description: EU and NATO membership (2004), euro adoption (2014), the 2008 financial crisis and severe recession, the ongoing debate over minority integration, Riga as European Capital of Culture (2014), and Latvia's response to Russian aggression in Ukraine.

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
